style: Read as a confident, energised product narrator for a short demo film — brisk, even and crystal-clear, always moving forward. Never draggy, never rushed; steady momentum with light, deliberate emphasis on the product names ClickHouse, Trigger.dev, Valhalla, on the word consultant, and on the payoff at the end. Short, clean pauses between sentences — not long ones.

beats.text: Where should you open a gym in Belgrade? Watch the answer draw itself.

No wall of text. A Trigger dot dev agent calls ClickHouse, tool by tool, and every result paints itself onto the map — rivals, an opportunity surface, the three best sites, a real ten-minute walk. The model never touches the geometry; it only says what the map cannot.

The top site is Rakovica — a dense residential edge with no gym anywhere nearby. The name is real boundary geometry, the numbers are what the score ranked on, and the walk reach was measured by Valhalla, on the actual streets. Not guessed.
But is that the only answer? No. This isn't a calculator — it's a consultant. Ask for the biggest markets instead, and the pins jump to the densest, most contested blocks in the city.
Ask where NOT to open, and it flags the saturated turf — over sixty gyms packed around a single block. A good consultant rules places out, too.
Or narrow the whole question to one neighbourhood — the six best spots inside Zemun alone, each named from real geometry, none of them invented. Local advice, from the same live data.

And it scales. Every food-and-drink venue in Belgrade — thousands of points, too big for the chat stream's one-megabyte cap. So it never enters it: it lands in ClickHouse, read straight from the browser.
Save a site — Postgres to ClickHouse in seconds, re-scored against seventy-five million live points.
One last thing — there's no web server. The entire app is a row in ClickHouse. Every file, a row you can query.
Ask a question, get a live map — not a wall of text. A consultant you can argue with, drawn from millions of points. That's WhereHouse.
